93.t: Bubbles' cramp rolls and heel drops
93.s: Green describes Bubbles' heel-dropping cramps, the kick cramp and the half-tempo time step called rhythm tap.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, it was -- he involved the heel, the dropping of the heels, you see, into what he called cramps, cramping, like that. And like what they call a break. Like after you do a step, you would do a break, and that's where he involved this cramping.

93.t: Why Bubbles' cramp roll was richer and progressive
93.s: The interviewers and Green compare the kick cramp to the walking cramp, noting more beats and use of the whole body, and that Bubbles invented it.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Much more, because he used the whole body. He used -- like he would jump. He would jump and hop, see, and by -- as he'd come down, as he'd land from the jump, he'd kick with the other foot, and the hop would come after the kick with the other foot, see. So --

93.s: They discuss how coming down on the heel as foot drum rested the dancer and differs from stabbing the heel.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: It was more restful to the tap dancer, because by them coming down from their toes or the ball of the foot onto the heel, it was just like he was standing up, see. And therefore, it was restful.

93.t: Kick cramp and Bill Bailey's walking cramp
93.s: Green demonstrates Bubbles' kick cramp and Bill Bailey's walking cramp, and says he now varies steps up to Take the A Train with the hoofers.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: So some years later I met Mr. Bill Bailey, and he had come along with a different way of doing a Bubbles tap step, which was a cramp. But Mr. Bailey did it down on the floor with the whole foot. He didn't kick it. He didn't kick the cramp. He

547.t: Mambo, cha cha, son montuno and tempo
547.s: How mambo, cha cha, and son montuno differ mostly by tempo and feel, with Puente and Prado examples.
547.q: Yes. It took me a long time to internalize that. Because we have terms like mambo. We have cha cha cha. We have son son montuno. Guaracha. What is all this? And a lot of it is the same rhythm but at a slower tempo. Like a mambo might be here [scats]. But then if you slow it down [scats] then it…

547.t: Swinging the eighth notes on percussion
547.s: Adapting congas and bongos to swing, Nat King Cole and Candido, and Chembo's remark about the clinic band.
547.q: It can. I’m sure you’re familiar like let’s say [scats] instead of playing straight eighths like on the conga [scats] you just swing it [scats]. And that’s one way you could get around it. The bongos, instead of going [scats].

547.s: The 6/8 feel of Rumba Colombia, with quinto and clave in two, and how long it took Rendón to understand.
547.q: Like we did “Rumba Colombia” [scats] 1-2-3-4-5-6; 1-2-3- 4-5-6. But then the quinto player is going [scats]. It’s like a different improvisation, it’s in two, it’s just in duple feel against the 6/8. And also we have the clave [scats] I can do the other part instead of doing this [scats]. That’s in…

1032.t: Does Afro-Cuban music swing? Ed Shaughnessy on swing
1032.s: She says the music is different, full of subdivisions and vibrations; Rowe quotes Ed Shaughnessy's definition of swing.
1032.q: It’s different. I mean it can in a way but you can hear that sort of underlying it but there’s always just the, a lot of the time in the music there’s so many subdivisions so rhythmically it’s more so like, it’s vibrations. There’s like just kind of I don’t know sometimes I felt very, very…

1032.s: Rowe describes struggling to hear the clave; she says it can be felt, and Cuban music came more quickly to her than swing pocket.
1032.ch: Playing, recording and making a living
1032.q: That’s so true, it really is. Yeah. Sometimes you can’t — you can feel it, and your body feels it, if something like goes off, right? It’s like having two left shoes on or something like that.

929.s: Allen asks how players get the New Orleans rhythm; DeVore says four-four and punch matter more than notes.
929.q: Well, for a New Orleans style band, the most important thing as far as rhythm is concerned is you're playing four-four time rather than two beat or any other times that bands have played. And the rhythm angle is the most important of all. I mean, even if a guy couldn't play a lick on a piano or a…

572.t: Rhythm names, afterbeat and the Smokey Mary drum feel
572.s: He says he had no special names for rhythms, explains the two-beat afterbeat and how his train-wheel rhythms led to Smokey Mary.
572.ch: Bucking contests, boogie woogie and rhythm
572.q: I, I just used that as, as, as, as a type. I didn't even know, oh, what to call it at that time. Uh-huh. Only when I wrote, wrote the story about it. Yeah. You see what I mean? It was different kind of a, of a feeling that I felt, uh, this, this rhythm would fit with the, uh, the wheels of, of, of,…

293.t: Band with Lemon and the need for swing
293.s: Playing with Lemon's band he told the leader to slow down and swing; recalls players such as Willie Paggio, Earl Wiggins and Thomas Jefferson.
293.q: Yeah, he was a white boy playing with him. He lives over the river somewhere. He's a good musician. George used to call it New Orleans, he's a great band. He sells instruments. He sells guitars, he sells amplifiers, he sells... He's out in Indianapolis. He's any play, any reeds, he's got a system…

510.s: He cannot define swing and calls it feeling, the same in swing and funk settings.
510.q: Feeling. It’s really funny you know. And I run across this every once in a while when I’m in an environment where there’s some heavy, heavy swingers, four-four swing type players, and some heavy syncopated Rhythm & Blues or Rock players. And how I feel on both of these environments you know. And I…

603.t: Timing, tempo and the punch line
603.s: Comic timing comes from musical tempo and rhythm.
603.q: Yeah. And that’s the application of the music too that’s so important to the tempo and rhythm and people will laugh at something that isn’t even funny if the tempo and the rhythm is right you know.

888.t: Teaching swing with movement and clapping on two and four
888.s: She teaches the whole-body feel of swing, using 'Pick Yourself Up' and clapping on two and four; she is called a physical singer.
888.q: Because I want them to understand that music involves the entire being, you know. It’s not just a spiritual thing, it’s not just a physical thing. It’s all of you. I mean every part of your being works with this and to get them to understand the concept of swinging, of the swinging. It’s clapping,…

458.t: Defining swing and the primacy of the beat
458.s: Swing is everything clicking; Beal says all music is about the beat and a conductor with the beat can survive.
458.q: Can I define swing? Swing is when everything is clicking and it’s intense and it feels good. What can I say? Everybody’s on the same plane.

397.t: Swing eighths versus straight Cuban articulation
397.s: He explains articulation differences between swing and Cuban rhythms such as cha-cha-cha, and why the feel must be learned.
397.q: Now we play the same tune Latin, like everybody calls it Latin and I don’t like that Latin, it’s Cuban rhythms, now you call that straight [counts/scats]. The articulation should be different. Should be different. And that’s what differentiates. But also what I have been doing, it’s something that…

439.t: Finding 'one' in Latin rhythms through dancing
439.s: Feeling comes before thinking; dancing helped with clave, and Jovino Santos Neto speaks of incorporating rhythm in the body.
439.q: You know that’s always, what you’re describing is always that conflict between the feeling and the thinking. Because what you feel is what you feel and nobody can argue with you. It’s always right, that’s what you feel. Now whether one person calls it “one” and another person calls it “four” that’s…

399.t: The clave inside Afro-Cuban musicians, and playing it with the foot
399.s: Rowe praises a video of Conte playing 3-2 clave with his foot; Conte explains the clave is internalized by anyone raised in the culture, even when nobody plays it.
399.q: Oh thank you. Yeah. You know because all that Cuban – if I’m playing congas and I’m playing authentic Cuban rhythms it all relates to the clave you know that. So I figured do a little bit of independence, put the clave in the foot and do that. I’m not the only guy that does that, a lot of the…

803.s: He likens swing to a language that must be internalised, and says it makes sense in New York and Harlem in a way it does not in Australia.
803.q: That’s true. It’s so complex. I really, it’s probably a common analogy but likening jazz and improvising to language, you know, and you can tell, having been spending some time in Spain and hearing the Spanish vocalists sing American tunes you know in one bar that they don’t speak English well…

131.s: Swing cannot be defined; Fats Waller and Ralph Sutton remarks.
131.q: Didn’t Fats Waller or somebody say if you have to ask that question you’ll never know or something like that.

931.t: Pop music becoming 'even eighth note' oriented
931.s: Rowe asks about Dodgion's remark; he explains the shift from swinging twelve-eight feel to even eighth notes.
931.ch: Early years and arriving in New York
931.q: Well some drummers, if you talk to some drummers, they might tell you that. Because that’s a basic thing. It’s an even eighth note as opposed to the twelve eight, smooth flowing.

1020.t: How the Birdland groove changed from Alex Acuna's version
1020.s: Erskine explains how Zawinul told him to stop the bossa nova feel and he found a fast shuffle.
1020.q: Well when I first joined the band I was playing it similar to the way Alex did. And just for the record when I heard that for the first time it was such a magical sounding recording and I told Jaco, I said, “This is the version of Weather Report I’ve been waiting for.” And I was fine, like just let…

693.t: His rhythm guitar monograph and what swing is
693.s: He describes his book on rhythm guitar and argues that swing cannot be forced, only allowed to happen.
693.ch: Swing, hot jazz and the bebop split
693.q: Well I’m writing a book, believe it or not, a monograph on rhythm guitar, the history of. Somebody asked me to do it and by the time I get finished with it I’ll have made a penny a page or something. Because it’s a labor of love. And in it I try to describe, first of all, to tackle those problems,…

59.s: Hyman says swing cannot be defined, but tempo matters, citing DJs and heartbeat.
59.q: No. It’s not possible. It’s not possible. It either swings or it doesn’t swing. But the right tempo is certainly the way to accomplish it. What the right tempo is is a matter of great debate and trial and error. I’m interested in one thing though. When I listen to, well even as far back as disco…

580.t: What makes a rhythm section swing
580.s: Israels explains swing problems as misaligned accents, criticises jazz education's two-and-four teaching, and uses a walking-against-gravity image.
580.q: Usually about a misalignment or a misalignment of accents or an imbalance of one kind or another. I often find that — we talked about jazz education earlier and there are a lot of people in the field of jazz education who are in a position, who are forced into a position of teaching about —…

935.t: Leading his own big band record and aiming the beat at the feet
935.s: Having free rein on the record; his aim to put a grin on the groove, and how audiences clap on one and three versus two and four.
935.q: Well, just to have some say-so in what’s going on in the music. I mean usually the drummer can take a certain amount of rhythmic charge. But when I’m a side man I do what I’m told obviously (sometimes I’ve been accused of certain things). But this time I had free reign to express myself and to put…

954.s: Swing is togetherness and how eighth notes are phrased, as he explains.
954.q: Yeah okay well I’ll try, now I’m understanding you better. To me, when people play together more, they’re in the same thought zone, that usually swings. And not that all swinging is the same, but it usually gets off the ground, I like to put it. You know what I mean? And it’s magic that happens.…

337.t: What does it mean to swing
337.s: He says swing is about time and cannot explain it.
337.q: That’s always been a hard thing to answer. I’ll tell you. It has a lot to do with timing, with time. See because the most important ingredient that anybody can have as a musician first is time. And you can have all the technique in the world but if you don’t have that time, which is, then forget…

1033.t: Samba, tempos and respecting lyrics and composers
1033.s: Samba makes everything better; she dislikes arrangements that contradict the lyrics or composer's intent.
1033.q: Well what I mean by that is that generally I don’t like to get too super far away from the composer’s original intention because those guys were brilliant, and mostly what I mean by it is when the lyrics are not taken into account. That drives me batty.

442.t: How swing turned into straight eighth notes
442.s: Morell speculates Latin music and the ease of shuffle feels shifted rhythm toward even eighths.
442.q: Yes somewhat. People ask me how do you think it got to where it was straight? Like straight eighth notes. Well I think perhaps Latin music is more eighth note based, like a cha cha, which is [scats] right? And that music kind of infiltrated the musical scene, right? And so the combination of the…

1031.t: Swinging versus playing with the time; Oscar Peterson and quotes from Frishberg and Redman
1031.s: Rowe says swing has become square. Pizzarelli talks about finding pianists who swing, Oscar Peterson, and reads quotes from Frishberg and Joshua Redman on the swinging blues.
1031.ch: Trio, swing and the piano players
1031.q: Well you know I had this conversation with Isaiah. And I was saying you know I get lucky because I manage to find piano players who want to swing, who want to play tunes, and participate in the band like that. I’ve heard — I mean I’ve been in bands where I’m the guy who’s trying to play rhythm…

947.t: Straight eighths and swing in rock and roll: Chuck Berry and Johnnie Johnson
947.s: Prompted by Bucky Pizzarelli, they discuss swing and straight eighths in early rock and roll, Chuck Berry and Johnnie Johnson.
947.ch: Learning to read, studio work and rock and roll feel
947.q: Ah. Well there you go, yeah. But you know Bucky, did he know, could he play “Dawn Go Away” by the Four Seasons by ear? I don’t think so. He wouldn’t want to. I think that’s more my —

487.t: Explaining the clave and finding the one
487.s: Clave never changes, the phrase does; conga patterns; why outsiders lose beat one and his own early confusion.
487.q: Yeah. And by the way, that also, the clave is the basis of how the conga player plays, because he’ll play two three [scats] boom boom. That boom boom is on the one, two, three. [Scats] So it all hooks up.

757.s: Both agree swing and the blues are essential; swing is a dotted-eighth heartbeat and jazz is about supporting colleagues.
757.ch: Jazz life and the state of jazz
757.q: Yeah. Well as do I frankly. I consider swing and having some familiarity with the blues — whatever that means — is essential in jazz and always has been. And I think one of the reasons is very human and very physical. And I think there’s a reason why 4/4 time or common time, or the people’s time…

358.s: Simmons explains why emphasis on the afterbeat rather than the downbeat makes music float and frees improvising, and how he uses it with singers.
358.q: and when I see the Africans dance, they’re still using afterbeats rather than the downbeat. They got that little extra beat in there when they dance you know, that was not in the European experience. And this affects the feeling of the music a great deal. And when I try to get people to get the…

618.s: He declines to define swing and says you point at examples.
618.q: You see what you do is you point. Point at examples. And point when it’s not happening. And then somebody with big ears could begin to say aha, I get it.

558.t: Bebo Valdes and the batanga rhythm
558.s: Batanga, created by Bebo in 1952 on Cadena Azul, combined conga and bata drums; it succeeded as music but not as a dance, despite Fellove's efforts.
558.ch: Tropicana, Bebo Valdes and the batanga
558.q: Yes, it was the combination of the conga and bata drums and very good arrangements. It began in 1952 on radio Cadena Azul. The rhythm Batanga. And Bebo was the composer and creator and the contributors were Trinidad Torregrosa who played the Iyá batá drum, Rolando Alfonso, Jesus and me. We were the…

107.t: Learning to swing in Detroit and defining swing
107.s: Foster says he learned swing gradually in Detroit, defines it as music that makes you tap on two and four, and says James McCarthy's playing sounded dull once he heard it.
107.q: No, no. It happened very naturally and very gradually over a period of time. It started with seeing something that I had never seen in Cincinnati, people sitting in the audience popping their fingers on two and four, two, three, four [Foster snaps a backbeat rhythm], and musicians doing the same…

108.t: What makes a band swing: tempo
108.s: The Savoy Sultans and Millinder found the right tempo; a Li'l Darlin' anecdote.
108.q: To me, like I said before, when the band is swinging, that’s when you can’t suppress the urge to shake your head or pat your feet. It isn’t always the tune. It has a lot sometimes to do with the volume or the particular mood they’re playing in. But, more than that, it has to do with the tempo, if…

373.t: What swing is: the pulse, from Bach to Mingus
373.s: Hentoff and Schoenberg agree that all music swings, and he describes jazz as a life force and being in the pocket.
373.q: It’s a pulse. I overuse the term, when I write about musicians, that jazz is a life force. You can tell if the music is swinging, if you can feel it. It doesn’t have to be explicit. People like Mingus, you could – implicitly, no matter what they were doing, you could feel that pulse, what I call…

953.t: Learning to swing: always part of his playing
953.s: He says he never had to learn to swing; rhythm and note placement were part of one package.
953.q: Well, by “swing”...you see, that’s hard. You have to define what you mean when you say “swing.” You, you have to define that more...

63.t: Fellow New Haven and big-band leaders; what 'swing' means
63.s: He lists those who became leaders (Spivak, the Dorseys, Miller, Goodman) and defines swing as the moment when the whole band is grooved.
63.ch: Early years: Cleveland, Aaronson, New York
63.q: Then Glenn came along. I came along before Glenn. Benny came first. No, Tommy came first. Tommy and Jimmy. Then they split up, and Tommy was the successful one. Then Benny came along with that terrible word, “swing,” as a noun or an adjective. It’s a verb. Swing music. If it doesn’t swing, it’s not…

379.t: Clave versus the four-beat jazz bar
379.s: He explains clave spans two bars, the downbeat is felt not played.
379.q: I say, well, that I cannot do nothing to change the pattern of rhythm. That's the way our rhythm is. You're supposed to (inaudible). Everything here is against the beat. American music, they give you all the big boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, but THIS music don't.

611.s: Waters explains that taking a 'Boston' meant a chorus played with a back beat on two and four, though he does not know where the name came from.
611.q: Yes, right, now, now. Yeah, now here's what this Boston is. This Boston, it specifies, see. It don't mean "take a chorus"; it means take a chorus, but it, the, but the type of rhythm is specified. When you play a Boston - you hear some of these Dixieland bands doin' it now - everybody has a back…

169.s: Patting rhythms on the leg, Klook's drumming and Feather's coinage of 'bebop'.
169.ch: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
169.q: Well, he took that feeling and made a beautiful sentence out of it, you know. And it was just a pat-your-lap kind of thing. You know, guys would go just... [MAKES SOUND]... I don't know whether that picks this up. Yeah, all kind of ways, you know. And if a guy could do something... We used…

389.t: The Jazz Age, swing and the shift from two-beat to eight-to-the-bar rhythm
389.s: He contrasts two-beat 1920s music and the later influence of Latin rhythms, and notes the shortage of early records.
389.q: But now that they're looking back on some of the early bands because they don't have too much recall for them; they don't have too many records. Swing -- from the swing period on, yeah, they got everything. But back in the 1920s you have to pick out a record here and pick out a record there, and…
